lesson.title: Branching on What a Value Looks Like
lesson.summary: The match statement checks a value against a series of patterns in order, running the block attached to the first pattern that fits, offering a cleaner alternative to long elif chains when you are really comparing one value against many possibilities.
lesson.body:
The match statement, introduced in Python 3.10, is another way of implementing a conditional statement, alongside if, if-else, and elif chains. Where an elif chain evaluates a fresh boolean expression at every step, a match statement is built around a single subject value that gets compared against a series of patterns, each introduced with the case keyword. Python checks the patterns in order from top to bottom and runs the block belonging to the first one that matches, then stops, exactly the way an elif chain stops at its first True condition. This makes match a strong fit whenever the real question is "which of these several specific values does this variable equal," rather than a set of unrelated boolean conditions.

Trace this example:

day = "Sat"
match day:
    case "Sat" | "Sun":
        print("Weekend")
    case "Mon" | "Tue" | "Wed" | "Thu" | "Fri":
        print("Weekday")
    case _:
        print("Not a valid day")

Python evaluates the subject, day, once, getting "Sat". It then checks the first case pattern, "Sat" | "Sun", which uses the pipe symbol to mean "matches either of these." Since day equals "Sat", this pattern matches immediately, so Python prints "Weekend" and skips every case below it, never even looking at the weekday pattern or the fallback. Had day instead been "Wed", the first pattern would fail to match, Python would move to the second case, find a match there, and print "Weekday" instead. The final case, an underscore by itself, is a wildcard pattern that matches anything at all, serving the same role the else clause plays at the end of an elif chain: a guaranteed catch-all for any value the earlier cases did not handle.

The same weekday logic could be written as an elif chain instead, comparing day == "Sat" or day == "Sun", and so on, and for this example both approaches are reasonable. Match statements tend to pull ahead once you are checking a single value against many specific possibilities, since the syntax states directly that you are comparing one subject against alternatives, rather than re-deriving that fact from a series of separately written equality checks. Match statements can also do more than compare exact values, including matching against the structure of a list or the type of an object, capabilities a plain elif chain does not have, though the day-of-week example above stays within the simpler, value-comparison use of the feature.

Because match is fundamentally a conditional statement, everything true of conditional statements in general still applies: exactly one case body runs (or none, if there is no wildcard and nothing matches), the body of each case is a normal indented block that can contain any statements, including further conditionals, and choosing match over an elif chain is a readability decision about your specific data, not a requirement imposed by the language.
